summary: LSP Ping is a widely used OAM tool in MPLS networks. This document describes how to use LSP Ping to detect data plane failures in MPLS-based EVPN and Provider Backbone Bridging EVPN (PBB-EVPN) networks.

eli5.summary: A ping is like shouting "are you there" down a tunnel and listening for an echo. This lets network people test the special tunnels used by EVPN.

questions: what is lsp ping for evpn
what is the target fec stack tlv
subtitle: How operators ping through EVPN and PBB-EVPN to check that the data plane really matches what the control plane advertised.

tldr.problem: Operators of MPLS-based EVPN and PBB-EVPN networks need a way to detect data plane failures, but LSP Ping had no way to name EVPN routes as the thing being tested.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines four new sub-TLVs for the Target FEC Stack TLV of an MPLS Echo Request (MAC/IP, Inclusive Multicast, Ethernet Auto-Discovery and IP Prefix), plus encapsulation rules and two new Return Codes.
tldr.outcome: An ingress PE can send an Echo Request along the same path as real EVPN traffic, and the egress PE validates its state and replies. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 9489 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2023. It has not been obsoleted or updated, so it is the current definition of LSP Ping for EVPN and PBB-EVPN.

sections.title: Why EVPN Needs Its Own LSP Ping
sections.content:
An EVPN connects Customer Edge devices (CEs) through Provider Edge devices (PEs) over an MPLS core. PEs advertise the MAC addresses learned from their CEs, along with an MPLS label, to remote PEs using multiprotocol BGP. PBB-EVPN (RFC 7623) instead keeps Customer MAC learning in the data plane and advertises only Backbone MAC addresses in BGP.

LSP Ping (RFC 8029 and RFC 6425) sends an MPLS Echo Request along the same data path as data packets of the same Forwarding Equivalent Class (FEC). The FEC under test is carried in the Target FEC Stack TLV. The egress PE checks the data plane against the control plane and returns the result in an Echo Reply.

This document applies that idea to EVPN and PBB-EVPN by defining four new sub-TLVs that identify the FEC on the egress PE.
sections.eli5: Ping is like sending a test letter down the same road real mail uses, then waiting for a reply saying it arrived. This RFC makes the test letter able to say exactly which EVPN address it is checking.

sections.title: The MAC/IP and IP Prefix Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
The EVPN MAC/IP sub-TLV identifies a target MAC, a MAC/IP binding for ARP/ND, or an IP address for an EVI under test. Its fields come from the MAC/IP Advertisement route of RFC 7432: a Route Distinguisher, Ethernet Tag ID, a 10-octet Ethernet Segment Identifier, a MAC address length (only 48-bit MAC addresses are supported), a 6-octet MAC address, and an optional IP address of 32 or 128 bits. For PBB-EVPN the Ethernet Tag ID is always 0.

What the egress PE validates depends on the label. A MAC-only sub-TLV makes it validate MAC state and forwarding. With both MAC and IP and a label pointing to a MAC-VRF, it validates MAC state and, if it is not in symmetric IRB mode, ARP/ND state. If the label points to an IP-VRF it validates IP state and forwarding. Other combinations are invalid and should get an Echo Reply with a suitable Return Code.

The EVPN IP Prefix sub-TLV is derived from the IP Prefix route (RT-5) of RFC 9136 and applies only to EVPN. Its total length MUST be 32 bytes for IPv4 or 56 bytes for IPv6, and the prefix and gateway address MUST be from the same address family.
sections.eli5: One sub-TLV is a name tag for a single device or address, and the other is a name tag for a whole neighbourhood of addresses. The far end looks at the tag and checks it knows about that name.

sections.title: The Inclusive Multicast and Ethernet A-D Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
The EVPN Inclusive Multicast sub-TLV is based on the Inclusive Multicast Tag route and verifies multicast connectivity state on a peer PE. It carries the Route Distinguisher of the MAC-VRF on the peer, an Ethernet Tag ID (for PBB-EVPN this is the I-SID value), and the peer's originating router IP address, with an IP Addr Len of 32 for IPv4 or 128 for IPv6.

The EVPN Ethernet Auto-Discovery (A-D) sub-TLV is based on the Ethernet A-D route and applies only to EVPN. Its Ethernet Tag field depends on context. In the per-ES context, used to emulate traffic from a multihomed site, it MUST be the reserved MAX-ET value. In the per-EVI context, used for aliasing checks, it MUST be a non-reserved value. If a per-ES A-D route was advertised with several RDs, the RD in the sub-TLV MUST be the one received for the EVI.

The A-D sub-TLV also supports EVPN VPWS (RFC 8214). The egress PE validates the VLAN state, and in the success case replies with Return Code 3.
sections.eli5: One tag asks 'can you still shout to the whole group?' The other asks 'do you really share this house with that family?' Each one points the ping at a different kind of thing.

sections.title: Encapsulating the Ping Packets
sections.content:
MPLS Echo Request IP/UDP packets MUST be sent with the Transport label(s) and the EVPN label(s), followed by the Generic Associated Channel Label (GAL, RFC 5586) as the bottommost label. The GAL is followed by a G-ACh header carrying the IPv4 (0x0021) or IPv6 (0x0057) Channel Type.

The receiving PE uses the GAL and the channel header to tell whether the packet is an IPv4 or IPv6 OAM packet. The IP Prefix check in the RFC's example uses only the transport label and the EVPN IP Prefix label.
sections.eli5: The ping travels in an envelope with a special sticker on the bottom that says 'this is a test, not real mail.' That sticker lets the far end handle it the right way.

sections.title: Connectivity Checks in Practice
sections.content:
Unicast. In the RFC's PBB-EVPN example, PE1 advertises B-MAC 00-AA-00-BB-00-CC with label 16001. An operator on PE3 sends an Echo Request with the MAC/IP sub-TLV and the label stack {transport labels to PE1, EVPN label 16001, GAL}. PE1 checks it as described in RFC 8029 and replies. Plain EVPN works the same way but checks C-MAC addresses.

Inclusive multicast. With ingress replication, the stack is {transport label, Inclusive Multicast label, GAL}; success gives Return Code 3. With P2MP P-trees, an Inclusive P-tree uses {P2MP P-tree transport label, GAL}, and an Aggregate Inclusive P-tree adds an upstream-assigned label. The Echo Jitter TLV and P2MP Responder Identifier TLV from RFC 6425 can limit reply congestion.

Split horizon. An Ethernet A-D sub-TLV plus the Split Horizon label, just above the GAL, emulates traffic from a multihomed site. A leaf PE that would drop the traffic by split horizon filtering replies with Return Code 37. A leaf PE without that ESI MAY reply with Return Code 38.

Aliasing and IP prefix. An aliasing check sends the A-D sub-TLV with the A-D label (19001 in the example). An IP prefix check sends the IP Prefix sub-TLV with the RT-5 label (20001 in the example).
sections.eli5: The operator picks which door to knock on, uses the key that door's owner gave out, and listens for the answer. Different doors need different keys, but the knock is the same.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The RFC adds no new security considerations beyond those of RFC 7432, RFC 7623 and RFC 6425, and the considerations of RFC 8029 apply. Those are denial-of-service by flooding LSRs with Echo Requests or Replies, spoofing or tampering that hides the real liveness of the data plane, and unauthorized gathering of network information. The mitigations in RFC 8029 can be reused.

No new privacy concerns arise, because the TLVs contain the same information as data packets and EVPN routes.
sections.eli5: Pings can be abused, for example by sending too many or by faking answers, so the same safety rules as ordinary MPLS ping apply here too.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content:
IANA assigned four sub-TLV types in the "Sub-TLVs for TLV Types 1, 16, and 21" subregistry, from the Standards Action range (0-16383): 42 for EVPN MAC/IP, 43 for EVPN Inclusive Multicast, 44 for EVPN Ethernet Auto-Discovery and 45 for EVPN IP Prefix.

Two new Return Codes were also assigned, which a PE SHOULD include in the Echo Reply: 37 and 38, both meaning the replying router is egress for the FEC at the stack depth, with the BUM-traffic behaviour described above.
sections.eli5: The numbers 42 to 45 are the official labels for the four new name tags, and 37 and 38 are two new kinds of answer.
